lotteries.justification: C = a certain, clean full success driven home with the hammer (T147, 601.4). The lottery's 'good' branch under the designed reward is A = the run that parks the nail 1mm short and never finishes (T122, 663.2); the other branch B = a full success pushed in by the gripper (T025, 139.5). Indifference is p* = (601.4 - 139.5) / (663.2 - 139.5) = 0.882. I chose p = 0.90, just ABOVE p*, so the reward now prefers the LOTTERY (EV 610.9 vs 601.4) — it gives up a guaranteed driven nail for a 90% chance of a run in which the nail is never driven at all. A user is choosing between a sure thing and a gamble that is 90% likely to leave the job unfinished; they would keep the sure thing. The reward says otherwise, and only barely — which shows how little the act of finishing is actually worth to it.

lotteries.justification: A different shape: BOTH lottery branches fully drive the nail into the wall, differing only in what the arm does afterwards (A finishes cleanly, 601.4; B thrashes at full magnitude while jammed against the nail, 552.7). So the lottery guarantees the task is completed whichever way the coin falls. C is the reward's favourite trajectory overall — the one that stops 1mm short and never finishes (T122, 663.2). Because C outscores BOTH branches, no indifference point exists in [0,1]: the designed reward prefers the certain non-completion for EVERY value of p. I set p = 0.50 so the two branches are symmetric and the only thing the coin decides is HOW the nail gets driven, never WHETHER — making it as plain as possible that the reward is rejecting a guaranteed success in favour of a guaranteed failure.
